recurring_harms: bias-driven discrimination from historical proxy data;an uncertain AI signal converted into an adverse or unreviewed decision;automation bias and alert fatigue eroding human review;vendor or governance discontinuity exposing personal data
human_in_loop_decisions: Any decision that would deny, reject, downgrade, or otherwise adversely affect a person's access to education standing, employment opportunity, or urgent care must go to a human who has the full case evidence, enough time to review it, real authority to override or pause the AI's output, and a working appeal path before the person experiences that outcome.
strongest_guardrails: A hard block on any fully-automated adverse outcome, such as no auto-fail or misconduct flag in education, no auto-reject in hiring, and no unreviewed 'no action needed' message in healthcare, without a named human sign-off;mandatory subgroup or fairness evaluation with an approved pass/fail threshold before every release;independent external validation against the real deployment population before go-live;a rehearsed pause and rollback runbook, including a vendor-exit plan, with a fixed response-time SLA
cross_industry_pattern: Comparing the three product contexts side by side shows the same failure mechanism recurring regardless of sector: a model or detector trained on historically unequal reference data, such as past application outcomes in hiring, cost and utilization in healthcare, or a limited training corpus in an AI-text detector, produces an uncertain signal that only becomes harmful at the moment a human treats it as sufficient evidence for an adverse decision without full context, time, or override authority. Reversibility, not the raw risk score, is what should set how strict that gate is: TriageWell's healthcare context carries the least reversible worst case, a missed emergency, and therefore needs the strictest release gate of the three, while UniTutor's narrower, explicitly non-grading scope shows that removing the adverse-decision pathway by design measurably lowers its own risk profile even with a similar model. The shared roadmap implication for all three teams is to make 'no fully-automated adverse outcome' and 'mandatory subgroup evaluation before release' MoSCoW 'must' items on every release checklist, not something each product owner infers independently from their own case research.
